title: Git branches and merging
goal: Work on a feature in its own branch, then merge it back into main cleanly.

concepts: What a branch is: a movable pointer to a commit
git branch, git switch -c feature-name, git switch main
HEAD: where you are right now
git merge: fast-forward vs merge commit
git log --oneline --graph --all to see branches
Deleting merged branches: git branch -d

resources.title: Pro Git: Branching in a nutshell
Pro Git: Basic branching and merging

build.task: In your jobready-journey repo, create day13/index.html with a simple 'My skills' page on main and commit it. Then create a branch add-dark-section, add a dark-themed 'Currently learning' section with 2 commits, and switch back to main. On main, make one commit that adds a footer. Merge add-dark-section into main (this creates a merge commit because main moved). Push main and the branch. Save the output of git log --oneline --graph --all to day13/graph.txt and commit it.
acceptance: Branch add-dark-section exists on GitHub with 2 commits of its own
main has a merge commit that joins the branch
day13/graph.txt shows the fork and the merge in the graph
Final page on main has both the footer and the dark section
Complete Learn Git Branching 'Introduction Sequence' levels 1–4 (note it in your commit message or progress log)

hints: Check where you are often: git status shows the current branch on its first line.
Order: git switch -c add-dark-section → edit, commit twice → git switch main → add footer, commit → git merge add-dark-section.
If git opens an editor for the merge message (Vim), type :wq and press Enter to accept the default message. To push a new branch: git push -u origin add-dark-section.
proof: Link to the merge commit on GitHub (open main's history and click the merge commit).

explainBack.q: Using your graph.txt, explain what a branch actually is and what happened when you merged.
lookFor: branch is a pointer/label to a commit
commits diverged because main got a footer commit

explainBack.q: When would a merge be a fast-forward instead of creating a merge commit?
lookFor: main has no new commits since the branch started
git just moves the main pointer forward

explainBack.q: Why do developers use branches instead of committing everything to main?

lastHintExplanation: A branch is just a named pointer to a commit; committing moves the pointer forward. When main and your branch both have new commits, git merge creates a merge commit with two parents that joins the histories. If main had no new commits, Git would fast-forward: just move main's pointer to the branch tip.

predict.q: You're on main. You run git switch -c feature, make 2 commits, then git switch main. What do you see in your files?
predict.why: Switching branches changes your files to match that branch's latest commit. The feature commits only exist on feature.

predict.q: main hasn't changed since you branched. You run git merge feature on main. What happens?
options: Fast-forward: main moves to feature's latest commit
predict.why: With no divergence, Git simply moves the main pointer forward.

concepts: What a pull request (PR) is: a request to merge a branch, with discussion
PR title and description: what changed, why, how to test
Reviewing your own diff on GitHub (Files changed tab)
Merge options: merge commit, squash, rebase (just know they exist)
Markdown: headings, lists, links, images, code blocks, tables
git pull to bring GitHub's changes to your computer

explainBack.q: What is the difference between a branch and a pull request?
lookFor: branch is a Git concept, a line of commits
PR is a GitHub feature to propose merging a branch

explainBack.q: After merging on GitHub, why did you need git pull on your laptop?
lookFor: pull = fetch + merge the remote changes

explainBack.q: Read out your PR description. Why does each part matter to a reviewer?
lookFor: how to check: steps to verify

lastHintExplanation: A branch is a Git line of work; a pull request is GitHub's page for proposing to merge that branch, with a diff, comments and a merge button. Merging on GitHub only changes GitHub's copy, so your laptop's main is behind until you git pull, which fetches new commits and merges them into your local branch.

predict.q: You merged a PR on GitHub. On your laptop you're on main and haven't pulled. You run git log --oneline. Do you see the merge commit?
predict.why: Your local repo only learns about new remote commits when you fetch or pull.

title: Merge conflicts: cause them, read them, fix them
goal: Create a merge conflict on purpose and resolve it calmly, so real ones don't scare you.

concepts: Why conflicts happen: the same lines changed differently on two branches
Conflict markers: <<<<<<< HEAD, =======, >>>>>>> branch
Resolving: edit the file to the final version, remove markers, git add, git commit
git merge --abort to back out
VS Code's merge editor buttons (Accept Current / Incoming / Both)
Avoiding conflicts: small branches, pull often

resources.title: GitHub Docs: Resolving a merge conflict using the command line

build.task: In day15/, create profile.md with lines: Name, City, Favourite language, Goal. Commit on main. Create branch city-update and change City and Goal; commit. Switch to main and change the same two lines differently; commit. Merge city-update into main and get a conflict. Resolve it by keeping City from the branch and writing a new Goal that combines both. Commit the merge. Then do it again with a second conflict and resolve it this time using VS Code's merge buttons. Write day15/conflicts.md explaining in your own words what each conflict marker meant.
acceptance: Two merge commits in history that resolved real conflicts
No leftover <<<<<<<, ======= or >>>>>>> markers in any committed file
Final profile.md has City from the branch and a combined Goal
conflicts.md explains HEAD, the ======= divider and the incoming branch section

hints: Git only conflicts when both sides changed the same lines (or neighbouring lines). Change City on both branches to different values.
When the conflict appears, run git status: files under 'both modified' need fixing. Open one and delete the markers, keeping the text you want.
After fixing: git add day15/profile.md, then git commit (no -m needed; Git suggests a merge message). Search the repo for <<<<<<< before committing.
proof: Link to one of your conflict-resolving merge commits.

explainBack.q: Using your conflict, explain what the text between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= was, and what came after.
lookFor: top section is the current branch (main/HEAD) version
bottom section is the incoming branch version

explainBack.q: Why didn't Git just pick one version automatically?
lookFor: Git can't know which meaning is right

explainBack.q: Name two habits that make conflicts rarer on a team.

lastHintExplanation: A conflict happens when two branches change the same lines differently. Git marks the spot: the section after <<<<<<< HEAD is your current branch's version, ======= divides it from the incoming branch's version ending at >>>>>>> branch-name. You edit the file into the final version, delete the markers, git add it, and commit the merge.

predict.q: Branch A changes line 1 of a file. Branch B changes line 20 of the same file. You merge B into A. What happens?
predict.why: Different, non-adjacent lines changed, so Git combines them automatically.

predict.q: During a conflict you run git merge --abort. What happens?
options: The merge is completed with your version
Everything goes back to how it was before the merge
predict.why: --abort cancels the merge and restores the pre-merge state.

title: How the web works: URLs, DNS, HTTP and DevTools Network
goal: Explain what happens between typing a URL and seeing a page, using real evidence from DevTools.

concepts: Client and server; what a URL is made of (protocol, domain, path, query)
DNS: turning a domain name into an IP address
HTTP request: method, URL, headers, body
HTTP response: status code, headers, body
Common status codes: 200, 301, 304, 404, 500
HTTPS and why the padlock matters
DevTools Network tab: waterfall, size, timing, headers

(2) Click the main HTML document request and copy its request method, status code, and 3 response headers you can explain. (3) Run nslookup (or ping) for that domain and record its IP. (4) Visit a page that doesn't exist on that site and record the status code. (5) Finish with a 10-step explanation, in your own words, of what happens from typing the URL to seeing the page. hints: Open DevTools → Network, tick 'Disable cache', then reload. The summary bar at the bottom shows requests, transferred size and load time. Click the 'Size' column to sort.
Headers worth explaining: content-type, cache-control, content-encoding, server, set-cookie. MDN has a page for each.

On Windows and Mac, nslookup example.com works in the terminal. Your 10 steps should mention DNS, the TCP/TLS connection, the request, the response, then the browser parsing HTML and requesting CSS/JS/images.

explainBack.q: Using your notes, explain what happened from typing the URL to seeing the page.
lookFor: browser parses HTML and fetches CSS/JS/images
uses their real numbers or site

explainBack.q: Explain one response header you recorded and why the server sent it.
lookFor: correct meaning (e.g. content-type tells browser how to treat the body)

explainBack.q: What is the difference between a 404 and a 500 status code?
lookFor: 404: resource not found, client asked for something missing

lastHintExplanation: The browser asks DNS for the domain's IP address, opens a connection (with TLS for HTTPS), and sends an HTTP GET request. The server replies with a status code, headers (like content-type: text/html) and the HTML body. The browser parses the HTML, then makes more requests for CSS, JS and images, and finally renders the page. 4xx codes mean the client asked for something wrong (404 not found); 5xx codes mean the server failed.

predict.q: A page loads 1 HTML file, 2 CSS files, 3 JS files and 10 images. How many HTTP requests (at minimum, with no cache) does it make?
predict.why: Each file is a separate request: 1 + 2 + 3 + 10 = 16.

predict.q: You reload a page and the Network tab shows status 304 for style.css. What does that mean?
options: Not Modified: the browser's cached copy is still valid
predict.why: 304 tells the browser to use its cached copy because nothing changed.

title: Positioning, z-index and pseudo-classes
goal: Place elements exactly where you want with position, control stacking with z-index, and style states with pseudo-classes.

concepts: position: static, relative, absolute, fixed, sticky
Absolute elements position against the nearest positioned ancestor
z-index and stacking contexts
Pseudo-classes: :hover, :focus-visible, :active, :nth-child(), :not()
Pseudo-elements: ::before, ::after, ::placeholder
inset: 0 as a shortcut for top/right/bottom/left

build.task: In day17/, build: (1) a product card with a 'SALE' badge pinned to its top-right corner using absolute positioning; (2) an image with a dark overlay and centred caption text on top (overlay with ::after or a div and inset: 0); (3) a modal: a 'Open details' link that targets #modal, where #modal:target shows a fixed full-screen backdrop with a centred box above everything (z-index); (4) a striped table using :nth-child(even); (5) clear :hover and :focus-visible styles on all links and buttons.
acceptance: SALE badge stays in the card's corner when the window resizes (card has position: relative)
Overlay covers the full image and the caption is readable
Modal opens via the #modal link, covers the page with a backdrop and closes with a close link
Table rows alternate colours using :nth-child
Tab through the page with the keyboard: every link/button shows a visible focus style

hints: If your badge flies to the corner of the whole page, the card is missing position: relative. Absolute elements look up the tree for the first ancestor that isn't static.
Overlay: .figure { position: relative } .figure::after { content: ''; position: absolute; inset: 0; background: rgb(0 0 0 / .5) }. ::after needs content to appear.
Modal with no JavaScript: #modal { display: none } #modal:target { display: grid; place-items: center; position: fixed; inset: 0; z-index: 100 }. The close link can be href="#".

explainBack.q: Your SALE badge uses position: absolute. Explain what it's positioned relative to and what happens if you remove position: relative from the card.
lookFor: without it, badge positions against a higher ancestor or the page

explainBack.q: What is the difference between :hover and ::after?
lookFor: pseudo-class selects an element in a state
pseudo-element creates/styles a part that isn't in the HTML

explainBack.q: Why is :focus-visible important for keyboard users?
lookFor: shows where focus is when tabbing
accessibility for people who don't use a mouse
removing outlines without a replacement makes pages unusable

lastHintExplanation: position: absolute removes an element from normal flow and positions it against the nearest ancestor that has a non-static position. That's why the card needs position: relative. A pseudo-class (:hover) selects an existing element in a particular state; a pseudo-element (::after) creates a styleable part that isn't in the HTML, and it only appears if content is set. Visible focus styles let keyboard users see where they are.

predict.q: A span has position: absolute; top: 0; right: 0. No ancestor has a position set. Where does it appear?
options: Top-right of the page (initial containing block)
predict.why: With no positioned ancestor, it positions against the initial containing block (the page).

predict.q: div::before { color: red } with no content property. What appears?
predict.why: ::before and ::after don't render without a content value.
